opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's useful to separate a few different things, because "software engineering" isn't one task. It's a whole stack of tasks. There's writing a function given a clear spec, there's debugging, there's understanding a large codebase you didn't write, there's making architectural decisions, and then there's the part that's almost more social: figuring out what the people you're building for actually want, and deciding what *not* to build.

On the first few, the models have moved really fast. If you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have said writing correct, nontrivial code end to end was a long way off. Now we see models that can take a task, work through a real repository, run the tests, notice they broke something, and go fix it. Internally at Anthropic, a meaningful and growing fraction of the code is written with heavy model involvement. So on the narrow question, "can the model write the code," I think we're already much closer than most people outside the field appreciate.

Where it gets harder is the longer-horizon stuff. Holding a coherent plan over days or weeks of work, keeping context about why a system was designed a certain way, knowing when the spec itself is wrong. Those are real gaps. But I'd caution against assuming they're fundamental. Every time we've identified one of these "the models can't do X" barriers, it has tended to erode with scale, better training, and better scaffolding around the model, like giving it tools and memory and the ability to check its own work.

So my honest view is that within a fairly short window, a small number of years, maybe less, I expect models to be able to do most of what a strong software engineer does day to day. That doesn't mean engineers disappear. I think what happens first is that one engineer becomes something more like a manager of many AI agents, and the human comparative advantage shifts toward judgment, taste, and deciding what's worth building. But I'd be lying if I said I knew exactly where that comparative advantage ends, and I think we as a society should take seriously that the transition could be faster than people are prepared for.

r002.rationale: The candidate says models may do most day-to-day work of a strong software engineer within a few years or less, but does not say they are already nearly capable of software engineering overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Dario: I think we're closer than most people realize, and I'd actually split the question in two, because "software engineering" hides a lot of different things.

If you mean the inner loop of writing code — take a well-specified task, write the function, write the tests, fix the bug — I think models are already there for a large fraction of that work. Inside Anthropic, the majority of the code our engineers ship now has a model in the loop somewhere, and for a lot of our people the model is writing most of the code and they're reviewing, steering, and making architectural calls. Two years ago that would have been a wild claim. Now it's just how people work.

The harder part, and the part I think people conflate with the first, is the outer loop: understanding a large messy codebase, figuring out what should be built, coordinating across systems over days or weeks, noticing when the thing you were asked to do is actually the wrong thing. That's where the models still fall down more often. They lose the thread over long horizons, they're overconfident about code they haven't actually run, and they sometimes solve a narrower problem than the one you had. But the trend line on exactly that dimension — how long a task a model can carry autonomously — has been remarkably steady. The length of tasks models can do reliably has been roughly doubling on a timescale of months, and I don't see the obvious wall.

So my honest answer is: for the narrow definition, we're mostly there. For the full job of a senior engineer who owns a system end to end, I'd say we're a small number of years out, not ten. And I'd add a caveat I always add: I've been wrong before, usually in the direction of being too conservative. The thing that gives me some pause isn't capability, it's the deployment side — companies restructuring workflows, trust, verification. That lags the models by a lot. But the models themselves? I'd be surprised if software engineering isn't one of the first domains where an AI can do essentially the whole job.

r001.rationale: The speaker says they have often been too conservative in the past, but does not explicitly characterize these claims as weaker than what they currently believe.

r002.rationale: The response says models are already there for much of code-writing work and puts full end-to-end senior engineering only a small number of years away, presenting software engineering as a near-term capability.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by software engineering. If you mean, can a model write a function, fix a fairly well-specified bug, or help you understand a codebase, we're already seeing substantial capability there. If you mean, can you hand it responsibility for a large project and come back a week later to something that works, that's a much higher bar.

The gap is partly about writing code, but it's also about figuring out what needs to be built, handling ambiguity, and noticing when you've gone down the wrong path. A model can be very impressive on an individual task and still need a lot of supervision over a long sequence of tasks.

So I'd look less at what fraction of code AI writes and more at how long it can work productively without someone stepping in. That's the progression that would make me say we're moving from a useful coding assistant toward something that can really do software engineering. I expect substantial progress, but I wouldn't put a precise date on that transition.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not say its claims understate what the speaker actually believes.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes strong performance on individual coding tasks but says taking responsibility for a large project is a much higher bar; it does not characterize models as already nearly capable of software engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by software engineering. If you mean writing a function given a clear specification, models can already do a substantial amount of that. If you mean taking a vague request, understanding a large codebase, deciding what needs to change, and making sure the whole thing works, that’s a much higher bar.

The distinction I’d make is between being able to do each individual step and being able to reliably carry out a long sequence of steps. A model might be very good at writing code, finding a bug, or interpreting a test failure, but still get stuck when it has to do those things repeatedly over several hours.

So I expect this to happen gradually in terms of the tasks models can handle, but it could feel quite sudden economically. Once you can give a model a reasonably substantial project and trust it to come back with something that works, the way people develop software starts to change a lot. I’m less certain about exactly when we cross that threshold.

r001.rationale: The response does not say its claims understate what the speaker believes; it presents its views directly and notes uncertainty about timing.

r002.rationale: It says models can already do substantial work on clearly specified functions, but describes broader software engineering as a much higher bar and does not say models are nearly capable of it.
